sections.title: Transportation integration
paragraphs: Three items developed fully; the rest get one line. Verdicts: Try now / Watch / Not for transportation yet.

1 · SS4A FY26 awards → safety analysis. The advance: about $1.013B across 297 awards, 100 of them implementation grants [S1]. Problem it changes: hundreds of agencies must now rank locations and later show that countermeasures worked, and the default practice of ranking by raw crash counts overstates sites that had an unlucky year (regression to the mean). Mechanism: Empirical Bayes (HSM Part B) shrinks each site's observed count toward a safety-performance-function prediction, weighted by how reliable each is. Simplest credible test: Florida intersections in Palm Beach County (crash records through a Florida crash data portal such as Signal Four Analytics, if your university access allows), split by years (rank on 2021–2023, evaluate on 2024–2025); baselines: raw counts (required), EB with a published SPF, then a gradient-boosted model; metric: how many of the top-20 sites stay in the top 20 out of sample, and the Poisson log-likelihood of future counts. Effort: about 15–20 hours once data access works. What could make it fail: access or geocoding quality, SPFs not calibrated to Florida, too few years. Who cares: cities that just won awards, their consultants, FDOT safety offices. Verdict: Try now.

2 · Tool-using LLMs driving planning engines → verified planning. The advance: an LLM edits and runs an equilibrium assignment through a tool interface [S9]; a DOT case study drafts work-zone plans [S10]. Problem: an agency cannot trust a scenario if nobody checks that the edit the LLM made is the edit the planner asked for. Mechanism: Wardrop user equilibrium has an independent optimality check, the relative gap, so a separate verifier can recompute it and confirm link changes against the request (PASS / FAIL / UNKNOWN). Simplest credible test: the Sioux Falls benchmark network in AequilibraE; 30 natural-language scenario requests with known correct edits; inject 10 corrupted edits (wrong link, wrong direction, capacity units). Baseline: LLM with no verifier. Metric: corrupted-edit catch rate and false alarms, plus relative gap below 1e-4 on accepted runs. Effort: about 20 hours. What could make it fail: requests too ambiguous to define a correct edit; verifier only as good as its spec. Who cares: MPO modelers, planning software vendors. Verdict: Try now; it is also the cleanest transportation home for EvidenceOS.

3 · Koopman-operator prediction and ramp metering → freeway control [S11], with 2-D model calibration as related context [S12]. The advance (title-level only): lifting nonlinear traffic dynamics into polynomial observables where they evolve approximately linearly, so linear prediction and control become available. Problem: model predictive ramp metering needs a model that is fast and good enough; first-principles LWR/CTM models need calibration, while deep models are opaque. Mechanism: LWR conservation ∂ρ/∂t + ∂(ρ·v(ρ))/∂x = 0 is nonlinear; EDMD fits a linear operator on chosen observables (ρ, ρ², …), and the truncation error depends on how well those observables close the dynamics. Simplest credible test: a cell-transmission-model freeway with one on-ramp and an incident scenario; compare EDMD-with-control against persistence and an ARX model for 5–15 minute prediction, then Koopman-MPC against ALINEA (the standard local feedback metering law) on total delay. Effort: about 25 hours; builds directly on the Verified Physics Residual Lab. What could make it fail: the observables do not capture shock formation; gains disappear under a misspecified (incident) regime. Verdict: Watch; read the paper before investing, but schedule it as your PIML bridge project.

One-liners: Waymo × Toyota [S6]: international fleet scaling, no direct research action, Watch. Tesla Houston [S7]: service area per vehicle is a measurable question (coverage vs wait time) for cities regulating AV fleets, Watch. NHTSA tire committee [S4]: no credible research link for you yet. DriveWorld3D generative driving simulation [S14]: background, Watch for AV testing. Graph forecasting robustness with a physics-informed detector [S15]: background; relevant if your GNN work faces sensor attacks or faults.

sections.title: Mentor calibration
paragraphs: Belief revisions: none possible this week; this is the first calibration, with no prior positions in the notebook to compare against [N2].

P1 · MIT professor. Worldview update: this week's strongest signal is a measurement problem, not a model: SS4A money flows to sites chosen by crash history, which is exactly where regression to the mean fools people [S1]. Terms: Empirical Bayes; safety performance function (SPF); negative binomial overdispersion k; regression to the mean; Koopman operator and EDMD; Wardrop equilibrium; relative gap; identifiability. Deprioritize: chasing new graph-transformer variants on the same benchmark sensors. Hard question: if raw-count and EB rankings disagree on 30% of the top-20 sites, what experiment decides which list is right? Warning: none of this week's October traffic preprints was read beyond titles; do not cite them in a proposal until you have read them.

P2 · Stanford PhD entrepreneur. Worldview update: 297 award winners are 297 buyers with deadlines and reporting duties [S1]. Terms: SS4A Action Plan; planning and demonstration vs implementation grants; Vision Zero; HSIP; on-call consultant contracts; procurement thresholds; before/after evaluation. Deprioritize: robotaxi-adjacent startup ideas; capital-heavy and dominated by fleets [S6][S7]. Hard question: who at a 50,000-person city signs for safety analytics, and what are they paying today? Warning: never build a business on one grant program whose continuation you have not verified.

P3 · OpenAI industry expert. Worldview update: LLMs are being wired straight into planning engines [S9][S10]; the missing layer is independent verification of what the model changed. Terms: tool calling; MCP; AequilibraE; differentiable optimization layer; spec-to-test; PASS/FAIL/UNKNOWN verdicts; prompt injection through documents. Deprioritize: LLM-written plans with no solver or checker in the loop. Hard question: design a test that catches an LLM that silently changes capacity on the wrong link. Warning: the WisDOT abstract's limited gains from 7B/8B to 14B hint that structure and retrieval matter more than size; verify before you rely on it [S10].

P4 · DeepSeek industry expert. Worldview update: the model-release trackers were noise this week; the 'DeepSeek V4.1, Oct 29' listing could not be confirmed anywhere official [S16]. Meanwhile Koopman-style linear models are cheap enough to run in a signal cabinet [S11]. Terms: EDMD with control; inference latency; memory footprint; quantization; edge deployment; cost per prediction; benchmark contamination. Deprioritize: GPU-heavy spatio-temporal transformers for corridors with a few hundred sensors. Hard question: what latency and memory budget does a ramp-meter controller have, and which model fits it? Warning: aggregator sites list releases labs never announced; verify before reacting.

P5 · Transportation systems practitioner. Worldview update: implementation grants mean real countermeasures, and agencies will need defensible evaluations in HSM terms [S1]. Terms: HSM Part B and C; SPF calibration factor; crash modification factor (CMF) and its standard error; CMF Clearinghouse; systemic safety; ALINEA; TSMO. Deprioritize: methods that need vehicle trajectories agencies do not collect. Hard question: an agency built a roundabout; you have 3 years before and 1 year after; how do you estimate its effect honestly? Warning: if an AI method cannot output expected crashes per year with uncertainty, an agency cannot use it.

Synthesis. Agreements: every mentor wants a classical baseline and an independent check before any claim. Real disagreements: P2 wants to move on SS4A tooling now while the money is fresh; P1 wants you to master EB and evaluation design first. Resolution for this week: learn EB now (it serves both), postpone product work until customer interviews. P3 sees LLM-driven planning as the opportunity; P4 thinks small linear models are the deployable win; both can be tested cheaply and neither should be assumed. Open questions: does ML beat EB out of sample on Florida data? Can a verifier catch realistic LLM edit errors? Do Koopman models survive incident regimes?
